name: Wampano
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible
sweep_summary: Wampano (wamp1250) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's only stress/accent/prosody-keyword title, Couper-Kuhlen 2001 'Interactional prosody: High onsets in reason-for-the-call turns' (Language in Society 30:29-53), is a Glottolog machine mis-attachment (record 674459 says 'assigned computationally from the term \"reason\"'): the Cambridge Core abstract (saved) shows it is conversation-analytic work on pitch onsets in radio phone-in calls, unrelated to Wampano or to word stress; full text paywalled (DOI 10.1017/S0047404501001026); priority none. Nothing read in this search of works with stress in the title or in the material already held by the project (Costa 2007 dialectology, Rudes 1998 etymologies, Trumbull 1873 Lord's Prayer notes, Pierson 1658 catechism) states where word stress falls in Wampano/Quiripi; Costa 2007 fn. 72 only says Abenaki Syncope in SNEA depends on 'currently ill-understood metrical factors (Ives Goddard, p.c.)'. The sole first-hand prosodic remark is Pierson's 1658 'To the Reader' note that his acute accent marks LENGTH and that disyllables are usually unmarked, 'being commonly of equal measure' -- not a stress statement. no DOI; Google Books API, scholar.archive.org, Semantic Scholar (not reachable by automated download) and OpenAlex (budget 0) gave nothing) and stays the high-priority acquisition target via library/JSTOR; whether it contains a stress statement is unverified.

earlier_scan.source_named: Only Costa 2007 (dialectology of Southern New England Algonquian) located; no phonological description of Wampano/Quiripi stress found

new_statements.quote: the accute or long accent thus noted (a) signifies that the sillable over which it is placed is to be pronounced long, the rest of the words be short, till the like, or a circumflex do regulate the sillables following. Words of two sillables most frequently be not accented at all, being commonly of equal measure, and hardly mispronounced.
new_statements.citation: Pierson, Abraham. 1658. Some Helps for the Indians: shewing them how to improve their natural reason, to know the true God, and the true Christian religion.. in the language of the Quiripi Indians of New Haven Colony. Cambridge [Mass.]: Samuel Green. Facsimile reprint with introduction by J. Hammond Trumbull, Hartford: Connecticut Historical Society, 1873.
new_statements.locator: 'To the Reader', unpaginated prefatory leaf following the title page of the 1658 original (reproduced in facsimile in Trumbull's 1873 reprint)
new_statements.reading: NOT a stress-placement statement. The only first-hand prosodic remark on Quiripi/Wampano: Pierson's acute 'accent' is an explicit LENGTH mark (the marked syllable 'pronounced long', the rest short, a circumflex resetting the pattern), and he says disyllabic words usually carry no mark because their syllables are 'of equal measure'. It says nothing about where word stress falls and cannot be used to code stress; the earlier reading already recorded it. No source read in this search of works with stress in the title states word-stress position for Wampano. Rudes 1997 (Anthropological Linguistics 39(1):1-59, the only phonological description) remains unread: JSTOR and HathiTrust search-inside both return an automated-access block challenges, no DOI, no open copy found.

sources.citation: Costa, David J. 2007. The Dialectology of Southern New England Algonquian. Papers of the 38th Algonquian Conference, 81-127.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Comparative phonology/dialectology of SNEA; Quiripi section pp. 117-119 covers dialect mixing, r/y variants and Pierson's chaotic vowel marking; Abenaki Syncope (pp. 96-100, fn. 72) said to depend on 'currently ill-understood metrical factors (Ives Goddard, p.c.)'. No statement of where word stress falls in Quiripi or any SNEA language.

sources.citation: Pierson, Abraham. 1658 [1873]. Some Helps for the Indians: A Catechism in the Language of the Quiripi Indians of New Haven Colony. Reprinted with an introduction by J. Hammond Trumbull. Hartford: Connecticut Historical Society.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Pierson's 'To the Reader' (orig. p. [3]) says his acute accent (á) marks a syllable 'to be pronounced long, the rest of the words be short', and that 'Words of two syllables most frequently be not accented at all, being commonly of equal measure' — a length/diacritic convention, not a stress rule. Trumbull's introduction (pp. 3-11) is on provenance and Pierson's poor grammar; nothing on accent.

sources.note: The only phonological description of Wampano/Quiripi (reconstructs the segmental system from Pierson 1658, Jefferson's Unquachog list and the Naugatuck vocabularies); if any published statement on Wampano stress exists it is here (Costa 2007 cites its pp. 20-21 for syncope, which in SNEA is metrically conditioned).
